newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FORECAST-Australian GDP growth seen slowing.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FORECAST-Australian GDP growth seen slowing.

text.p: Australian economic growth should slow in the year to September, adding support to calls for another rate cut, although many economists see the second half of 1996 as the likely low point in the economic growth cycle.

With most of the partial indicators that are fed into GDP spreadsheets already released, the median forecast of economists surveyed by Reuters for the average measure of GDP, GDP(A), is for a 0.9 percent rise for the September quarter.
September quarter GDP data is due on Wednesday.

Of the measures used to calculate GDP(A), expenditure based GDP is seen as the strongest in the quarter, with the median forecast being for a 1.2 percent rise, while income and production based GDP are both seen rising by around 0.8 percent.

Quarterly forecasts were marked up after the release of stronger than expected third quarter inventories data on Monday. Prior to the news of the 2.3 percent rise in inventories, GDP(A) forecasts had centred on quarterly growth of 0.6 percent.

While the quarterly GDP rise will be stronger than the 0.1 percent seen in the June quarter, in annual terms the growth rate is expected to slow to around 3.4 percent from 4.5 percent in the year to June, due to the 2.0 percent rise in the September 1995 quarter dropping out of annual calculations.

Economists said that while the slowing annual growth would support expectations of a third interest rate cut following the 0.5 percentage point cuts on July 31 and November 6, the September quarter data was historical, telling them where the economy had been, not necessarily where it was heading.

"Part of the problem is that the September quarter data still reflects largely the uncertainty running into the August budget and was too early to pick up any material benefit from the first official cash rate cut at the end of July," UBS Australia chief economist Stephen Roberts said.
Despite the slowing in the pace of activity, the annual growth rate will still be around the level many see as close to the economy's potential rate.

Macquarie Bank economists, who are at the top end of expectations for GDP growth, said assesssing the underlying pace of economic activity in 1996 had been made difficult because of the quarter-to-quarter volatility in GDP estimates and the mixed nature of growth across sectors.

While the stocks build up in the September quarter has lifted forecasts, the unwinding of the build up should keep growth subdued in the December quarter, economists said, with the end result being that the second half of 1996 could mark the low point of growth in this cycle.
The slowing in annual growth, despite the fact it remains above three percent, would also keep hopes of another interest rate cut alive.

"An outcome in line with our forecast (0.9 percent) is unlikely to be a big surprise to markets, although it may underpin talk of further rate cuts," Bankers Trust Australia seior economist Peter Munckton said.
However, while the market may run with the idea of a rate cut, economists said the clues for monetary policy changes lay elsewhere.

Nomura Research senior economist Andrew Pease said that investment intentions of firms released last week meant that regardless of the GDP result, the Reserve Bank was unlikely to believe the economy was in danger of entering a recession.

"Rather, the Reserve Bank will cut interest rates further if it believes that inflation is going to remain low and the unemployment rate can be reduced without creating inflationary pressures," he said.
